design_detail: Narrative clinical review with two illustrative case vignettes, by four stroke clinicians at Harborview Medical Center, University of Washington (Front Neurol 2024;15:1397677; received 8 March, accepted 8 April 2024). Sections: US and global epidemiology of methamphetamine use; haemorrhagic stroke (vignette of a 47-year-old man with a basal-ganglia haemorrhage; epidemiology; pathophysiology; treatment and outcomes); ischaemic stroke (vignette of a 33-year-old man with a middle cerebral artery occlusion and vasospasm; epidemiology; pathophysiology; acute treatment); diagnosis, cessation and withdrawal. No methods section: no search strategy, eligibility criteria or appraisal. 106 references. Five figures (CT and angiography images of the two vignettes; two mechanism schematics). Read as the published version deposited in PMC.
can_establish: How stroke clinicians in a western US centre summarized, in 2024, the observational and case literature on methamphetamine and haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke, which primary studies carry each statement, and where they judged the evidence weak (vasculitis, ischaemic stroke, acute treatment).
cannot_establish: The size of any stroke risk attributable to methamphetamine, because sources were not systematically identified or appraised, the two risk estimates cited are given without intervals or covariates, and the two vignettes are single cases in which other causes (untreated hypertension; an unmonitored cardiac source) were not excluded.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited stroke evidence: two hospital-database studies of stroke risk (Westover et al. 2007; Huang et al. 2016), single-centre cohorts comparing methamphetamine-positive and negative patients with intracerebral haemorrhage (Swor et al. 2019, n=41; Zhu et al. 2020, n=61) or ischaemic stroke (Zhu et al. 2023), aneurysm series (Beadell et al. 2012; Moon et al. 2015; Noblett et al. 2021; Caton et al. 2022), autopsy series (Citron et al. 1970; Karch et al. 1999; Darke et al. 2018), case reports, the Lappin et al. 2017 review, and rodent and monkey experiments. Two patients from the authors' centre are described as vignettes.
sample.demographics: Vignettes: a 47-year-old man with untreated hypertension and a urine screen positive for methamphetamine; a 33-year-old man with a urine screen positive for methamphetamine and no further use history. Young is used for patients under 50 in the abstract.
sample.selection_effects: Selection of sources is unstated. The review leans on hospital series from the western United States, where the authors note methamphetamine use has historically been highest. The vignettes were chosen to illustrate, not sampled.

exposure.measurement: Not described at review level. The review notes that urine toxicology detects methamphetamine for up to about 4 days, that amphetamine immunoassays have many false positives (some antihistamines, decongestants, bupropion, trazodone, chlorpromazine, promethazine, a labetalol metabolite), that confirmation by LC–MS separates true from false positives, and that history is unreliable: in Zhu et al. (2020), 29 of 379 (7.7%) people with haemorrhagic stroke who denied methamphetamine use screened positive (Diagnostic challenges and management, 1st–2nd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. The authors state that route of administration is rarely reported and that its effect on risk is unclear; dose and duration are not reported by the aneurysmal haemorrhage outcome studies. In the vignettes, use history was unclear or not documented.
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed as a limitation: the aneurysmal haemorrhage outcome studies are said to be hampered by high rates of polysubstance use; reversible cerebral vasoconstriction and PRES cases attributed to methamphetamine occurred with other substances; people who use methamphetamine are more likely to use nicotine, cannabis, cocaine, opioids and other drugs (Introduction › Epidemiology, 4th paragraph). Not otherwise handled.

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. Cited comparisons: methamphetamine-negative patients with intracerebral haemorrhage (Swor; Zhu 2020), age-matched controls with aneurysmal haemorrhage (Beadell), people without methamphetamine use with aneurysmal haemorrhage (Moon; Caton), propensity-matched ischaemic stroke controls (Zhu 2023), hospitalized controls in Westover and Huang.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review notes that methamphetamine-associated haemorrhage occurs in younger people with fewer comorbidities but higher smoking rates; pre-existing aneurysms, untreated hypertension and smoking are discussed as contributors but no cited study is said to have measured them before use began.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable at review level. Outcomes discussed: incidence of intracerebral and subarachnoid haemorrhage and ischaemic stroke; haemorrhage location; aneurysm size and morphology; NIHSS, GCS, ICH score, modified Rankin Scale, Glasgow Outcome Scale; ischaemic stroke subtype; white-matter hyperintensities; cardiomyopathy, ventricular thrombus, QTc, atrial fibrillation, endocarditis side.
outcomes.operationalization: Methamphetamine-related stroke is not defined; in the vignettes it means a stroke with a positive urine screen for methamphetamine.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Second-hand figures: methamphetamine raises the likelihood of intracerebral haemorrhage by as much as 2–5 times (refs 11, 37: Huang et al.; Westover et al.; no intervals); among people who used methamphetamine in Huang et al., incidence of subarachnoid haemorrhage 6.2 and of intracerebral haemorrhage 20.8 per 100,000 person-years (no comparison-group rates given); aneurysmal haemorrhage outcomes worse with methamphetamine: median Glasgow Outcome Score 3 versus 5 at discharge (p<0.001; Beadell), OR 5 (95% CI 1.03 to 24) at 1 year and OR 7.2 (1.2 to 30) at 3 years (Moon); ischaemic stroke subtypes in people with versus without methamphetamine use 31% vs 28% small-vessel, 25% vs 24% large-vessel, 34% vs 46% cardioembolic (not significant; Zhu 2023); ventricular thrombus in 10 of 30 people with methamphetamine cardiomyopathy (Schürer); QTc prolongation in 27% of 158 people who used methamphetamine (Haning & Goebert); 86% higher risk of a diagnosis of atrial fibrillation in a 2022 California database analysis; relapse in 61% of 350 people within a year of treatment (Brecht & Herbeck).
analysis.covariates: Not reported for any second-hand estimate except that the white-matter association is described as independent of other cardiovascular risk factors and the Moon association as independent.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed (no eligibility criteria). The review does report null and conflicting findings: no association with ischaemic stroke in the two population studies, no outcome difference in the larger intracerebral haemorrhage cohort, no change in mean arterial pressure with chronic methamphetamine in small animals, no necrotizing angiitis in two autopsy series.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Haemorrhagic stroke is the best-documented association: two hospital-database studies (one of amphetamine-use codes) with estimates of about 2 to 5, case series in which over 80% of reported methamphetamine-associated strokes were haemorrhagic, and single-centre cohorts showing that methamphetamine-associated intracerebral haemorrhage occurs in younger patients, mostly in deep (hypertensive-pattern) locations. The evidence for vasculitis is weak (one 1970 polysubstance series; two autopsy series without necrotizing angiitis), the population studies found no association with ischaemic stroke, outcome comparisons conflict, and acute-treatment evidence consists of case reports.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion states that methamphetamine "poses a clear risk of hemorrhagic stroke", a causal formulation resting on two observational database studies without intervals in the review. The abstract says methamphetamine may partly explain rising stroke rates in the young and calls it an increasingly prevalent cause of strokes in young patients, while the Introduction concedes that the cited trends in substance use among young people with stroke (4.4% to 28.9% in one registry) were not specific to methamphetamine and no methamphetamine-specific trend is presented. The conclusion says patients with methamphetamine-related stroke have a greater increase in disability; the cited cohort found no difference in discharge function or mortality, only a larger change from pre-stroke mRS, which follows from better pre-stroke function. The abstract describes the literature as case studies and series, while the body also relies on cohort and database studies. The haemorrhagic vignette is attributed to methamphetamine in a 47-year-old with untreated hypertension in whom MRI was not done because the cause was not felt to be in question; the ischaemic vignette is attributed to methamphetamine-induced vasospasm, though the spasm was seen during catheter instrumentation and long-term cardiac monitoring was not performed. Against this, the review is careful on vasculitis (to be invoked rarely and with skepticism), on ischaemic stroke and on treatment; the gap lies in the abstract and conclusion, two of whose statements (disability, rising contribution to stroke in the young) are not supported by the evidence the body cites.

timeline.event: Citron et al. necrotizing angiitis series: 14 people who injected several drugs, 12 reporting methamphetamine, 1 exclusively; the basis of the vasculitis hypothesis, judged weak by this review
Karch, Stephens & Ho: over 400 San Francisco deaths with methamphetamine detected, no necrotizing angiitis at autopsy (as reported here)
Westover et al. population-based hospital study, ages 18–44: amphetamine use and haemorrhagic stroke; no association with ischaemic stroke

Huang et al. 10-year Taiwanese cohort of people who used methamphetamine: haemorrhagic stroke increased; incidence 20.8 (intracerebral) and 6.2 (subarachnoid) per 100,000 person-years; no association with ischaemic stroke
Lappin, Darke & Farrell review of 98 published cases: over 80% haemorrhagic (cited here as ref 13)
Darke, Lappin, Kaye & Duflou national study of 38 fatal methamphetamine-related strokes in Australia: no necrotizing angiitis (as reported here)
Zhu et al. single-centre cohort of 61 methamphetamine-associated intracerebral haemorrhages: younger, deep locations, no difference in discharge outcome or mortality

replication.where_it_stands: Consistent with Lappin et al. (2017) on the predominance of haemorrhagic stroke, and more sceptical than that review about vasculitis as a mechanism. The risk estimates it cites (Westover 2007; Huang 2016) and the outcome cohorts (Swor 2019; Zhu 2020; Beadell 2012; Moon 2015) need their own cards before any claim of magnitude; Lappin 2017 and this review cite overlapping sources and are not independent support.

funding.funder: No financial support received for the research, authorship or publication (Funding Statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: None: the authors declare no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors at Harborview Medical Center, University of Washington, Seattle (stroke neurology). Two first authors contributed equally. Peer reviewers and editor are named on the article.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young adults that verifies methamphetamine exposure by confirmed toxicology and history, with a comparison group matched on smoking, hypertension and other drug use, reporting incidence of intracerebral haemorrhage, aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage and ischaemic stroke as absolute rates with intervals; for treatment, a registry of thrombolysis and thrombectomy outcomes in patients with confirmed methamphetamine exposure.

domains.note: No methods section of any kind: no search, dates, databases or inclusion criteria, and no statement of how the 106 references were chosen.

Several cited bodies of work are appraised in the text: the 1970 necrotizing-angiitis series is called a limited basis for extrapolation, the aneurysmal-haemorrhage outcome studies are said to be hampered by small samples, selection bias, polysubstance use and missing dose and duration, and the studies suggesting ethnic differences are called small and selected. But the headline epidemiological figures are passed on without design, interval or adjustment (2 to 5 times for intracerebral haemorrhage; up to 6.5 times for stroke in people who use drugs; 86% higher odds of atrial fibrillation, taken from a two-page editorial; over 80% of published cases haemorrhagic).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Only the two case vignettes come from the authors' own centre. No reference in the list is authored by any of the four authors.

The body marks speculation as such (aneurysm growth after a single case, the plausibility of chronic hypertension, stroke risk after cessation "not clearly documented"). The abstract and Conclusion do not: methamphetamine "poses a clear risk of hemorrhagic stroke", haemorrhagic stroke is "the more common type" of complication, and greater disability is stated as fact and attributed to the younger age of the population, where the body reports no difference in discharge function or mortality and only a greater change in modified Rankin Scale score.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a methamphetamine-stroke link
domains.note: The body is even-handed: it reports the null and conflicting results (no difference in blood pressure, ICU stay or discharge outcome in the larger intracerebral-haemorrhage cohort; no necrotizing angiitis in over 400 autopsies or in 38 fatal methamphetamine-related strokes; no consensus on vasospasm or Hunt and Hess grades; a paucity of epidemiological evidence for ischaemic stroke). The under-represented side is in the abstract and Conclusion, which carry the adverse readings only.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3), so the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The review makes no claim to be systematic and has no methods, which fixes the first domain at high and therefore the overall judgment at high, since the overall can be no milder than the worst domain. Within that limit the review is a careful one: it appraises the weakest literature it cites, draws on no work of its own, and hedges its mechanisms, but its abstract and conclusion state more than its body supports. It may be cited for the map of stroke-specific cohorts published since Lappin et al. (2017), for its scepticism about vasculitis and for the clinical points on toxicology and withdrawal; every number in it must be taken from the primary source, and it is not evidence for the relative frequency of haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine is said to raise the likelihood of intracerebral haemorrhage by as much as 2–5 times (refs 11, 37: Huang et al. 2016; Westover et al. 2007). In Huang et al.'s 10-year cohort, incidence among people who used methamphetamine was 6.2 per 100,000 person-years for subarachnoid haemorrhage and 20.8 for intracerebral haemorrhage. Over 80% of methamphetamine-related strokes in published case reports and series were haemorrhagic (Lappin et al. 2017).
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke › Epidemiology & characteristics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: No intervals or comparison-group rates are given. As reported in Lappin et al. (2017, Table 3), Westover's estimate (OR 4.95) concerns amphetamine use and haemorrhagic stroke, and Huang's (HR 2.09) haemorrhagic stroke.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine-related haemorrhagic stroke is described as affecting younger people with better pre-stroke function and fewer comorbidities (cited to Lappin et al. 2017, Swor et al. 2019 and Zhu et al. 2020) and more often men (Lappin 2017 and Zhu 2020); lower rates of hypertension and antithrombotic use and higher rates of smoking come from Zhu et al. (2020) alone, and of these only the smoking difference is described as significant. Haemorrhages are mostly deep (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons), with significantly less lobar involvement than non-methamphetamine haemorrhage in the largest single-centre cohort.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke › Epidemiology & characteristics, 2nd–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Subarachnoid haemorrhage with methamphetamine use is usually aneurysmal and occurs at younger ages; in 23 patients with methamphetamine-associated aneurysmal haemorrhage, aneurysm type and location did not differ from patients without methamphetamine exposure, but aspect ratio was larger (Caton et al. 2022). Whether vasospasm or Hunt–Hess grade differ is unsettled.
key_findings.locator: Epidemiology & characteristics, 4th paragraph; Pathophysiology of hemorrhagic stroke, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Vasculitis: the hypothesis rests on Citron et al. (1970), 14 people who injected several drugs, 12 reporting methamphetamine and only 1 exclusively; 4 fatal cases described in detail (2 with confirmed and 1 with possible methamphetamine use), diagnosed mostly from other organs. Rhesus monkeys given methamphetamine showed calibre changes, perivascular infiltration and microaneurysms but no clear necrotizing arteritis. Over 400 San Francisco autopsies with methamphetamine detected and an Australian study of 38 fatal methamphetamine-related strokes found no necrotizing angiitis. The authors conclude vasculitis should be invoked rarely and with skepticism.
key_findings.locator: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Chronic hypertension as a pathway is poorly documented: chronic methamphetamine did not change mean arterial pressure in small-animal studies; methamphetamine use was associated with more white-matter hyperintensities independent of other cardiovascular risk factors (Zhu et al. 2023).
key_findings.locator: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Aneurysm size: in 62 people with intracranial aneurysms and methamphetamine use, ruptured aneurysms had a median diameter of 5.5 mm (mean 6.3 mm) (Noblett et al. 2021); the authors set this against a meta-analytic mean of 6.1 mm for ruptured aneurysms in general, so size alone does not show higher rupture risk with methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Outcomes after intracerebral haemorrhage conflict: methamphetamine-positive patients (n = 41) had higher mean arterial and diastolic pressure, more days of intravenous antihypertensives and longer ICU and hospital stays (Swor et al. 2019); in a slightly larger cohort (n = 61) there was no difference in blood pressure, ICU or hospital stay, NIHSS, GCS, ICH score, discharge function or mortality, though more participants underwent surgery (Zhu et al. 2020). The review states, citing both studies, that the change in modified Rankin Scale score from pre-stroke to discharge was greater in the methamphetamine group, that is, a larger worsening of disability, since the scale rises with disability.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic considerations & outcomes in meth-related hemorrhagic stroke, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage with methamphetamine use: median Glasgow Outcome Score at discharge 3 versus 5 in age-matched controls (p<0.001; Beadell et al. 2012); worse outcome at 1 year, OR 5 (95% CI 1.03 to 24), and at 3 years, OR 7.2 (95% CI 1.2 to 30) (Moon et al. 2015). The authors note small samples, selection bias, polysubstance use and no dose or duration data.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic considerations & outcomes in meth-related hemorrhagic stroke, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The 3-year interval is not symmetric around 7.2 on the log scale (geometric midpoint about 6.0, editors' calculation); this may reflect an exact interval or rounding; check in Moon et al.

key_findings.finding: Ischaemic stroke: incidence with methamphetamine use is unknown; the two population-based studies (Westover; Huang) found no statistical association, and both identified cohorts by ICD codes among hospitalized patients. In a California single-centre comparison of ischaemic stroke admissions, subtypes did not differ (small-vessel 31% vs 28%, large-vessel 25% vs 24%, cardioembolic 34% vs 46%), but microvascular ischaemic disease on MRI was greater than in propensity-matched controls (Zhu et al. 2023).

Cardioembolic pathways cited: ventricular thrombi in 10 of 30 (33%) people with methamphetamine cardiomyopathy and reduced ejection fraction (Schürer et al. 2017); QTc prolongation as the commonest ECG abnormality, 27% of 158 people who used methamphetamine (Haning & Goebert 2007); 86% higher risk of atrial fibrillation diagnosis in a 2022 California database analysis; among people injecting stimulants (75% methamphetamine), endocarditis was evenly left- and right-sided, versus 66% right-sided among people injecting opioids (Johnstone et al. 2022).
key_findings.locator: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related ischemic stroke, 2nd–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Acute ischaemic stroke treatment evidence in people who use methamphetamine consists of one case report of intravenous thrombolysis (a woman with carotid dissection, NIHSS 21, alteplase within 80 minutes, with improvement), a 29-patient cocaine-positive series without thrombolysis complications, and isolated thrombectomy and angioplasty case reports; the authors recommend standard therapies for eligible patients and warn against bias related to substance use.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic considerations in methamphetamine ischemic stroke, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Among patients with haemorrhagic stroke who denied methamphetamine use, 29 of 379 (7.7%) screened positive for amphetamines after exclusion of recent false-positive medications (Zhu et al. 2020); urine screens detect methamphetamine for up to about 4 days.

Stopping methamphetamine is associated with reversal of cardiac dysfunction (moderate-strength evidence, Manja et al. 2023 systematic review); reduced stroke risk after stopping is described as reasonable but not documented. In 350 people treated in Los Angeles, 61% relapsed within the first year (Brecht & Herbeck 2014).

Vignettes: a 47-year-old man with untreated hypertension, systolic pressure over 250 mm Hg and a 7.4 × 4.5 × 5.1 cm left basal-ganglia haemorrhage, urine screen positive for methamphetamine, use history unclear, discharged with mRS 4; a 33-year-old man with a right middle cerebral artery occlusion (NIHSS 15), urine screen positive, treated with thrombolysis and thrombectomy, with vasospasm during catheter access and in MCA branches that improved after intra-arterial milrinone, otherwise unremarkable work-up (2 days of telemetry; no long-term cardiac monitoring), attributed to methamphetamine-induced vasospasm.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke › Case vignette; Methamphetamine-related ischemic stroke › Case vignette; Figures 1, 3, 4 (images)

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal time course as the review gives it: an early crash of 12 to 24 hours with exhaustion and fatigue, a withdrawal phase of 2 to 4 weeks with depressive symptoms, increased sleeping and eating, and an extinction phase of up to 6 to 12 months with continuing cognitive and mood changes. The review notes that this period can overlap stroke recovery, making the cause of new mood or mental-status changes hard to tell apart.
key_findings.note: Second-hand: cited to references 105 and 106, Acheson et al. (2023) and the 2009 Cochrane review of treatment for amphetamine withdrawal. The same phases appear in acheson_2023 (Introduction), itself citing earlier sources, so the figures should be traced to the primary studies before use.

reporting_issues.issue: The regional shares of US methamphetamine drug submissions in 2022 are given as 39% West, 33% South, 29% Midwest and 8% Northeast, which sum to 109%, and 39% is called the majority.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one figure is wrong; the NFLIS 2022 report should be used directly for any regional claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The review states that people who used methamphetamine in the US in 2015–2019 were 50.9% women (citing Han et al. 2021); this encyclopedia's card for Han et al. (first-pass) records 50.9% women as the weighted composition of the whole survey sample of 195,711 adults, not of people who used methamphetamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a misattribution; the sex distribution of people who use methamphetamine must be taken from Han et al. directly.

reporting_issues.issue: Stroke risk among people using drugs is said to be as high as 6.5 times that of people who do not use drugs, cited to Kaku and Lowenstein (1990) (Introduction › Epidemiology ¶5). The first reader recorded that Lappin et al. (2017, Table 3) give the same study's relative risks as 6.5 for ischaemic and 11.7 for haemorrhagic stroke at ages 35 and below; that comparison is outside this source and has not been re-checked by the second reader.
reporting_issues.consequence: Kaku and Lowenstein must be read before either figure is used, and the 6.5 should not be carried as a methamphetamine-specific or stroke-type-specific estimate. The Lappin figures remain single-reader.

reporting_issues.issue: The 86% higher risk of atrial fibrillation is attributed to a 2022 California database analysis but cited to ref 85, which by title and length (3 pages) is an editorial comment, not the database study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The primary analysis is not cited; the figure cannot be checked from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that cardiotoxicity occurs with acute, chronic and binge use and that severity of use independently predicts outcomes (Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related ischemic stroke ¶2, last sentence) is cited to references 12 and 86-88: a case report of myocardial infarction with normal coronary arteries, an echocardiographic comparison of young people with cardiomyopathy, and a study of binge administration whose title names no species. None of the three concerns severity of use as a predictor of outcomes. The first reader also recorded that the corresponding sentence in Kevil et al. (2019), reference 12, carries no citation of its own; that is outside this source and has not been re-checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim that severity of use predicts outcomes has no traceable support in the references given here, and should not be carried into a monograph without a primary source.

reporting_issues.issue: Two case reports described as involving methamphetamine (refs 92 and 94) are titled as amphetamine-induced cardiomyopathy and amphetamine-induced arterial occlusion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The substance in these cases should be checked before they are counted as methamphetamine cases.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2-to-5-fold figure is worded as methamphetamine increasing the likelihood of intracerebral haemorrhage (Epidemiology & characteristics ¶1), with no interval, no adjustment and no design given, and one of its two citations (reference 37) is titled for amphetamines or cocaine rather than methamphetamine. The first reader additionally recorded, from Lappin et al. (2017), that the underlying estimates are for haemorrhagic stroke generally rather than intracerebral haemorrhage; that lies outside this source and has not been re-checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable as a causal or intracerebral-haemorrhage-specific estimate; the primary studies (references 11 and 37) are needed, and the stroke-type question stays open until Lappin et al. is read.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's statement that haemorrhagic rather than ischaemic stroke is the more common neurovascular complication of methamphetamine use rests on the share of published case reports and series (over 80% haemorrhagic, cited to Lappin et al. 2017, at Epidemiology & characteristics ¶1). The population studies the review cites give relative risks against people who do not use methamphetamine, not the ratio of haemorrhagic to ischaemic stroke among people who do, and the review itself notes a paucity of epidemiological evidence for ischaemic stroke.
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of published cases reflects what gets written up, not relative incidence. No monograph should state that haemorrhagic stroke is the more common type on this basis; the same inference appears in sc_paulus_2020 and both cards now carry the caveat.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC11076881 (published version; all sections including both case vignettes, figure legends, author contributions, funding and conflict-of-interest statements, article notes and the full reference list; Figures 1–5 are images and were not extracted; no tables; no supplementary material)

disagreements.first_pass: Methamphetamine-associated intracerebral haemorrhage affects younger patients with better pre-stroke function and fewer comorbidities, more often men, with lower rates of hypertension and antithrombotic use and higher rates of smoking (Zhu et al. 2020); haemorrhages are mostly deep (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons), with less lobar involvement than in non-methamphetamine haemorrhage in the largest single-centre cohort.
disagreements.reviewer: attribution is narrower than the source: refs 13, 38 and 39 for younger age, better pre-stroke function and fewer comorbidities, refs 13 and 39 for male predominance, ref 39 alone for hypertension, antithrombotics and smoking, of which only smoking is significant
disagreements.resolution: Rewritten. Checked at Epidemiology & characteristics ¶2: the first clause carries three citations (13, 38, 39), male predominance two (13, 39), and only the hypertension, antithrombotic and smoking comparison is attributed to reference 39 (Zhu et al. 2020), with "significantly higher" used of smoking alone. The card had given the whole sentence to Zhu et al. (2020). Locator (¶2-3) is right and unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke, 5th paragraph
disagreements.reviewer: the content is exact but sits in Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke ¶4; the card counts the Figure 2 legend as a paragraph
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 4th paragraph. Counting only running text, the section runs: hypertensive surge (¶1), vasospasm and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction (¶2), blood-brain-barrier breakdown (¶3), vasculitis (¶4), chronic hypertension and white-matter hyperintensities (¶5), aneurysms (¶6). The Figure 2 legend between ¶1 and ¶2 is a caption, not a paragraph (locator convention, docs/VERIFICATION-BRIEF.md).

disagreements.first_pass: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke, 6th paragraph
disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed; the location is ¶5 by text paragraphs, the card having counted the Figure 2 legend
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 5th paragraph, by the same recount. Content re-checked there: no change in mean arterial pressure with chronic methamphetamine in small-animal work (reference 65, a rat study of cardiovascular and respiratory function), and more white-matter hyperintensities independent of other cardiovascular risk factors (reference 66, Zhu et al.).

disagreements.first_pass: Outcomes after intracerebral haemorrhage conflict: methamphetamine-positive patients (n=41) had higher mean arterial and diastolic pressure, more days of intravenous antihypertensives and longer ICU and hospital stays (Swor et al. 2019); in a larger cohort (n=61), there was no difference in blood pressure, ICU or hospital stay, NIHSS, GCS, ICH score, discharge function or mortality, but more surgery and a larger fall from pre-stroke mRS (Zhu et al. 2020).
disagreements.reviewer: two fixes: 'a larger fall from pre-stroke mRS' should be a larger worsening (increase), and the mRS point is cited to refs 38 and 39 together, not to Zhu 2020 alone
disagreements.resolution: Both accepted and rewritten. Checked at Therapeutic considerations & outcomes ¶2: the sentence on the change from pre-morbid to discharge modified Rankin Scale score carries references 38 and 39 together, and the modified Rankin Scale rises with disability, so a word meaning a decrease reversed the meaning of the result. The n = 41 and n = 61 figures are confirmed, as is the review's misprint of IV hypertensive agents for antihypertensives.

disagreements.first_pass: Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related ischemic stroke, 3rd–4th paragraphs
disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed; the location is ¶2-3 by text paragraphs, the card having counted the Figure 5 legend
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to the 2nd and 3rd paragraphs. The section has three paragraphs of running text (atherosclerosis; cardioembolic sources; infective endocarditis), with the Figure 5 legend between the first and second. All four figures re-checked there: 10 of 30 with ventricular thrombi, QTc prolongation in 27% of 158, an 86% higher risk of atrial fibrillation diagnosis, and the left- and right-sided endocarditis comparison.

disagreements.first_pass: Stroke risk among people using drugs is said to be as high as 6.5 times that of people who do not use drugs (Kaku & Lowenstein 1990); Lappin et al. (2017, Table 3) report the same study's relative risks as 6.5 for ischaemic and 11.7 for haemorrhagic stroke at ages 35 and below.
disagreements.reviewer: partly-confirmed: the review's side is confirmed (Introduction › Epidemiology ¶5: up to 6.5 times, ref 9, Kaku & Lowenstein 1990), but the figures attributed to Lappin et al. (2017, Table 3) come from another paper and could not be checked
disagreements.resolution: Reworded rather than removed. Confirmed in this source: the 6.5-fold figure is in Introduction › Epidemiology ¶5 with reference 9, and the reference list gives reference 9 as Kaku and Lowenstein (1990). The Lappin Table 3 comparison is in another paper, which this reading did not cover and which no reader has re-checked, so the issue now says so and the card no longer asserts it as verified.

disagreements.first_pass: The statement that cardiotoxicity occurs with acute, chronic and binge use and that severity of use independently predicts outcome is cited to Kevil et al. (2019), where the corresponding sentence carries no citation, and to a case report, an echocardiographic comparison and a rat binge-dosing study (refs 86–88), none of which by title concerns severity of use as a predictor.
disagreements.reviewer: partly-confirmed: the citation set and the titles of 86-88 are confirmed; that the sentence in Kevil et al. (2019) carries no citation, and that ref 88 is a rat study, could not be checked here
disagreements.resolution: Reworded. Confirmed from the source and its reference list: reference 86 is a case report of methamphetamine-associated myocardial infarction with normal coronary arteries, 87 an echocardiographic comparison in young adults with cardiomyopathy, 88 a study of binge administration whose title names no species (so the card no longer calls it a rat study), and none addresses severity of use as a predictor. disagreements.resolution: Re-appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist (METHODS §5.3, modelled on sc_kish_2017). AMSTAR 2 is for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and scoring a narrative review against it only restates that it is not systematic. My own five judgments, made from the text, agree with the second reader's: no methods or search (high); real but uneven appraisal of the cited studies, with the headline risk figures passed on unappraised (some concerns); nothing of the authors' own cited (low); speculation marked in the body but not in the abstract or conclusion (some concerns); the balance of adverse against null findings even in the body but not in the abstract or conclusion (some concerns). Overall high, the worst domain. The substance of the earlier reasoning, that every number must be taken from the primary source, is kept.
